Neon Abyss is a unique and slightly awkwardly positioned Roguelike indie game. You can see the imitation and blend of many famous Roguelike gameplay but also will experience a rather strange sense of déjà vu in the game.

The game has a fun and sophisticated pixel art style, different props and weapons, a variety of game mechanics and level design, and a novel pet system. Neon Abyss certainly has its characteristics and allows players to experience a different Roguelike game experience. The game allows players to make highly customizable choices for their routes, allowing players with different playing styles to flexibly choose their strategies.

But this work is not satisfactory. Whether it's the lack of introduction to the game's mechanics and equipment, the repetitive and long-playing game design, or the unbalanced and overly dependent on luck prop design, these really easy to stimulate the player's sense of boredom and displeasure. For players using the handle, the game using the right stick aiming and shooting operation may take a long time to adapt, and the production team focused on the free Neon Abyss: Infinite mobile version of the decision is also quite unfavorable to the PC players to get a good gaming experience. In addition to weapons, props, and modes, even the mobile version has been added to the multiplayer online play mode. Players who paid for the PC version seem to be treated like outcasts - at least for now.

I only recommend Neon Abyss to those who have not played too many Roguelike games. Most of the players with more exposure to Roguelike games have strong opinions about this game, and the game itself is not overly innovative in terms of gameplay. Given that the game's mobile version is free, has more fully updated content, and has a multiplayer mode, I really can't think of any advantages of the PC version at the moment.

The majority of reviews on here are positive with like a few hours or even less which I'd say is misleading. I was very close to posting this review earlier on but I wanted to make sure I wasn't missing something by not beating the last 2 bosses, turns out there wasn't much. 

[h1]This game becomes a huge grind that's priced higher than BoI:Rebirth or Enter The Gungeon with significantly less replayability and substance[/h1]

While learning the ropes the game play is initially enjoyable but ends up being sub par. Seems awesome in the trailer, unfortunately each of those mini game rooms are all gated behind dozens of hours of playtime with the horribly implemented boss coin system, which I've only gotten far enough to even unlock two as the progression constantly comes to a halt. I just got on the third page of the six having already beaten the game needing the next character to further the tree anywhere else, he's shot up to 30 coins to unlock. You get 1 coin per boss so at best you can only get 8 or 9 per run which totals up to 4 runs for just one tier of progress. I haven't even completed everything on each of the first two pages either, there's a lot of items cluttering the tree that have almost no use in the game, nobody is spamming grenades to kill enemies as they're typically a rare resource for accessing rooms or items. Yet there's a bunch that build off of this alone, which didn't synergize with my rocket launcher or explosive bullets. There's no way to speed this up other than to maybe throw runs halfway to farm the first couple of bosses which makes it more of a grind. Upping or lowering the difficulty does not change the amount of coins at all and only arbitrarily changes enemies hp a bit. That's all, no other incentive to ever up it to hard mode so I wouldn't even bother with it as long as I did as it just makes runs take longer, and get more repetitive.

The enemies are almost the exact same throughout the most of the game, they change color and tweak the attack they do as new forms. So there's barely any variety on them except for maybe 1 or 2 new ones the first time you get to floor 5. The game is set up in such a way even when you know what you're doing you may just take damage regardless, walk in a room without a giant overpowered weapon that kills everything instantly? Well once you pass floor 5 almost every enemy does contact damage where previously almost none did, so some awkward room layouts where you have nowhere to go but forward get you damaged if you're not killing everything instantly. But if you do have that room clearing monster of a gun, which really isn't that hard since every item upgrades your gun is the same making the bullets bigger, you won't typically be able to see your character or the enemy and their bullets that slip right through to hit you.

Even if you aren't disadvantaged in either way you may take damage regardless, because there's an enemy from the early game that teleports right in front of you to smack you with its third upgraded form. Instead of being really slow and having to hit you directly, he now does contact damage, teleports faster, and also fires diagonal shots after. So when you enter rooms where you can't even see the entirety of them he may spawn off screen so you can't see him, immediately go into his teleport and then appear in front of you when you didn't even know he was in there. They also have this Wisdom/ Violence mechanic similar to Isaacs devil/ angel deals where you can get a progress bar going in the bottom right to earn access to a bonus room with items in them. This was a good concept where one of them rewarded playing well if only it's implementation wasn't so counter intuitive. They describe it as some kind of choice between the two with Wisdom being the harder one since you can't take any damage clearing rooms to progress it, and Violence being easier as all you need to do is take damage on each room but risk losing more health. 

However this isn't the case, very often you end up forced down violence as all of the weapons, items, and familiars you get are out to ruin any chance you have at going for Wisdom points, if you yourself directly damage one of the big purple Wisdom crystals, chests, or doors in the game they'll immediately turn Violence red which happens to deplete all Wisdom progress you've made, and turns it into a Violence bar. There's effectively no way to reduce Violence other than using an aforementioned Wisdom crystal, but the reduction is so small comparatively and enemies can even hit these things as they spawn in any room. So it's unreliable and faster to just complete an unintentional Violence bar rather than try to get rid of it, luckily it doesn't take your current progress away when enemies do so it only ruins your chances to further the Wisdom you were going for. If you try to play around this, your familiars still exist to keep firing away at enemies that spawned so you must pray none tag a chest, crystal, or door so you can still use them. The game also requires you to repeatedly complete either of these to try and spawn a token in the deal room through pure RNG that only then allows access to the 4th or 5th boss every run, akin to Isaac with the polaroid. Losing any progress at no fault of your own for even just one more chance getting there when succeeding 4 or 5 times over the course of a run sometimes isn't enough is very frustrating. A simple fix would be to have these faded out until a room was cleared and they became interactable.

On that note the eggs as a whole are a bait after you've seen every pet as you don't ever really need them and should avoid picking any up for the few good pets some may have as others are actually detrimental. There's also like less than 25 guns in this game since I see the same ones all the time, which wouldn't be too bad if the majority weren't unusable meme guns. It's literally better to stick with the default weapon a lot of the time compared to how weak most are, despite their bullets appearance. Half of them randomly fire lasers which awkwardly can't be adjusted once firing, the previously mentioned rockets ended up doing pathetic damage despite being heavily upgraded and half of what was fired would still miss while homing in. If you played Gungeon and had the complaint of using the pistol for managing ammo it's arguably worse here as there's few exceptions to switch off the starter gun since most are a downgrade and underwhelming. 

I've already seen every single room layout time and time again, bosses quickly become very easy and the things that would provide the variety this game desperately needed are all time gated. There's also day one DLC which you have to pay for if you're not persuaded to get this during it's launch week. I'd only recommend this game on sale at below it's launch price, 15$ if you like cosmetics in your roguelikes more than variety, 10$ for maybe a reasonably priced game for what's currently available. If you still want to play this I'd recommend the free demo as I put in maybe 8 hours there before this released, you can experience the combat and there's a few unlocks I've yet to get here in that challenge mode. And let me tell you that you're not missing much if you've played a roguelike that does a proper job of blending the repetition with replayabliity. Adding on the demo and taking away a bunch of hours I left this on I got burned out half way through but was determined to finish it, so you get maybe 20 hours out of this which isn't bad, except other games can have 100+ for less money where it's more of a challenge than grind. I'd say despite some of the flaws it's a 5 or a 6/10 as there was clearly effort put in with some unique concepts but there's not much depth once the novelty wears off, even changing some things I don't really have a desire to keep playing other than to try and get more out of it.

Neon Abyss has the potential to become a great game, but it is not there yet. While I have had a lot of fun playing so far, I would definitely recommend waiting for an update before buying the game. 
I'll try and list out some of the things I like and the things that I think really need to be addressed before the game is worth buying.
Pros:
-I like the idea of gun leveling. This makes it so that even the starting gun can be a viable weapon and also creates a feel of progression even if using the same gun for a whole run.
-I like the basis of the angel and devil system and I think that being able to choose which path to go for makes for an interesting game mechanic.

Cons: 
-The level and enemy variety are extremely small. It is basically impossible to tell what level you are on without looking at the transitions between levels. 

-The unlock system is not very fun. Unlocking things is done by using yellow crystals which drop whenever you defeat a boss. The cheapest that an unlock costs is 5 crystals and many two times that. With a full run bringing about 7-9, that means that sometimes it can take forever to unlock even a single item. Beyond that unlocking items this way isn't very interesting and makes progression feels too grindy (as opposed to objective-based unlocks like in the Binding of Isaac).

-I am not a fan of the egg system. Eggs hatch into tiny companions that have a variety of effects. The problem with the system is that the effectiveness of these companions vary and are sometimes actually actively harm your run. In addition, you get so many eggs in a single run that it is hard to really keep track of which companions you have. This also makes it very hard to intentionally keep them alive or use them in any meaningful way.  The eggs seem like something that could be an interesting mechanic, but ended up being something that I ended up mostly ignoring.

-The chest system seems very unbalanced. Both keys and bombs are a scarce resource on many runs and spending an entire key or bomb in order to open a chest seems like it should be pretty rewarding, but chests never seem to contain anything worth the price. Using up valuable resources only to get an egg or a couple purple crystals makes it so that the trade is rarely, if ever, worth it.

-Upgrades lack oomph. The most useful upgrades are usually just straight up stat increases. Apart from the popcorn item that causes your bullets to explode or the item that creates a mine every time you jump, there seems to be a severe lack of "zaniness". Yes you have upgrades that give you flight or extra jumps, but too many of them seem to be "give you random consumable if you get enough kills or when your egg or pets hatch." Most upgrades have very little change on the feel of a run and if it weren't for how each different gun acts, it would be hard to tell one run from another. 

-This may sound like a small issue but the angel system seems too delicate. It only takes a single shot to turn an any angel device, door, or chest into its devil form. This would be fine except for the fact that enemy bullets also affect them too, meaning that even if you avoid shooting at them, they may still be changed just because an enemy shot at you.

Smaller Issues:
-The use key is bound to the same button as melee attack. This wouldn't be a big problem if it weren't for the fact that angel devices turn into devil devices on a single hit. This has caused me on multiple occasions to attack the angel device when I am actually trying to activate it.

-Without upgrades most characters have very little movement options. This is a problem because a lot of the boss patterns seem to be balanced in a way that makes it extremely hard to avoid hits without movement upgrades.
-Active abilities are directly tied to guns. This is more personal preference but I feel like this definitely affects run variety, as there are many guns that either don't have an active ability or the ability is not worth using in most cases. 

-The hitbox to collect items is too small. In order to pick up an item you have to be at the same exact level as the item. This is  most noticeable when you have flight and can only pick up coins with your feet.




tldr: Neon Abyss has potential but is held back by a severe lack of variety and poorly implemented mechanics. With a few changes the game become one of the greats but I would not recommend buying the game in its current state.

TL:DR;
Too short and frustrating, devs has a lot to fix gameplay/balancing-wise

At first inspection, this is a really fun and interesting roguelite. A lot of synergy with weapons and equipment, each equipment showing up on your character to make each run aesthethically unique. Some mechanics like weapon levels and eggs which further helps the game to stick out from the other roguelites.

But- The game needs A LOT of tuning to make it worth your time.
-I mentioned the game has a lot of synergy between weapons and equipment. while true, it also has a lot of equipment which contradict or ruin other equipment. Prime example would be popcorn and the silver ball pet. Popcorn makes each bullet you shoot explode, and the ball is a pet that rotates around you and block bullets. The ball doesnt just block enemy bullets, but yours aswell, and if you have popcorn the blocked bullets will explode right in your face and damage you. This would be fine if the game had any way to drop equipment or dismiss pets, but that doesnt seem to have been implemented.
-The game is really short, even with the gating the game forces on you. Each time you defeat an unique boss, you have to start over, which unlocks another floor for the next run. Even with the gating you can "finish" the game in a couple of hours. Usually with roguelites you have to die and upgrade your character or unlock new loot so you can make it further the next round, but is completely unnecessary here. The unlock-tree has a lot to offer, but you'll usually be done with the game before you've even finished the first tab in the tree (game has atleast 3 tabs). 
-Difficulty is useless. Increasing the difficulty doesnt make the game any more interesting, or reward you in any way. It just seems to change the enemies' health and damage done, and you'll still be rewarded 1 upgrade token per boss killed. Highest difficulty is also locked behind the talent tree for some reason.
-Invincibility on enemies doesn't make them harder, just slows down gameplay, which in turn makes it boring. There is no fun in having to wait for an enemy to make an action in order to kill it. It baffles me that these stone enemies spawn so frequently once you unlock the second talent tree. It just turn the game into a turn-based game, rather than a semi-fastpaced platform shooter. The fact that harder enemies are locked behind the talent tree is also ridiculous, as it would entice that you actually make the game MORE difficult by upgrading yourself, instead of easier.
-Unavoidable damage. Whenever you enter a room, you should be able to atleast somewhat establish yourself into the environment and see what you're up against so you have a chance to dodge anything that gets thrown at you. In here however, mobs can sometimes spawn right up in your face, and even bosses can just hit you right as it spawns in (like the god of racing if your down a couple of floors already).
-Pets. Some are just terrible companions. The mechanic in itself is a nice addition, but there's no way to handle the pets. Some just steal your loot, some block your bullets, and some throw you around. Why should i even pick up eggs if theres a chance it will just damage me?

Recap of what the devs should fix:
-Synergy.
-Game length.
-Reward higher difficulty.
-Enemy invincibility is a terrible mechanic, incredibly overused.
-Unavoidable damage when entering room.
-Pets are assholes.

At first I enjoyed this game as its sorta 'my first rogue like' in that its very easy and fast to play compared to other rogue likes. Unfortunately this ends up becoming an issue in the long run, with the small item pool of relatively basic items, lack of enemy types, and simple structure the game ends up becoming a bit boring. This is not the real issue though, it would still make a fun quick play if it wasn't for the bugs. Sometimes 'Free Trial' items just do not work, enemies will sometimes become invincible or locked into one of their two modes, items will not be able to be picked up and these issues mixed with the very vanilla gameplay/synergies leads you to playing near identical runs hindered by bugs every 2-3 playthroughs. Certain pets will block explosive weapons, melee even on the sword character is basically useless and minigames/bosses are incredibly repetitive(sometimes you'll play the same keyboard song 3 times in a row). With a mixture of vanilla rogue like play, bugs and questionable game design Neon Abyss feels like a game that just misses the bullseye in being something great.

[h1]Positives[/h1]
[list]
[*]Permanent progression looks interesting at a glance. I didn't see all of the upgrades yet, but among the ones I've there are none of those boring "+2% damage".
[*]Characters (their abilities) are interesting. To give a few examples: a sword (as 2ndary weapon), dodge-roll ability, Damaging dash ability (needs to be timed), ability to fly.
[*]Good selection of weapons and a long list of upgrades (a lot of them are very similar buffs though).
[*]Creative non-combat rooms.
[*]Art style. It's the colors of this game that first got me to notice it.
[/list]

[h1]Negatives[/h1]
[b]Mobility always feels off[/b]
This one's might be subjective and I can't explain it, but mobility often feels insufficient, or maybe just wrong. Movement is responsive and not too slow, but it feels off even with movement speed upgrades.

Certain upgrades can also give you the ability to fly and that turns the combat much easier, but mobility in flight is even worse. It's almost like it's a static movement speed and not controlled by momentum.

[b]Problems with combat[/b]
Most of these issues weight heaviest at the start of the run and are somewhat  "fixed" by the middle of the run, as you collect upgrades.
[list]
[*]Starter weapon (same each time) has slow projectiles, low fire rate and and barely deals any damage. 
[*]Enemies (even basic ones) feel bullet spongy until considerable amount of upgrades are collected. 
You'll launch a laser show at 1 basic enemy and it survives for 2-5 seconds (that feels like a lot).
[*]No damage numbers. It's not a problem for many games, but this game features slow weapons, quick weapons and upgrades for those weapons. There's no way to compare a sniper rifle to a machine gun, or how different upgrades affect them.
[*]Mobility problem. It is usually not a problem in terms of evasion, but it just adds to clunky/slow feel.
[/list]

[b]Screen Clutter[/b]
This is by far the worst offender. As you progress through your run and collect upgrades, weapons start firing more (in a spread) projectiles, they get bigger and fire rate increases. At some point your own projectiles start completely blocking your vision and avoiding small stray attacks becomes incredibly difficult. Once you upgrade your weapons basic enemies are a much bigger threat than bosses.

During most of gameplay when you are clearing rooms, armored enemies (they block attacks) become difficult to kill, because it becomes hard to see if an enemy is open, and if it took damage when you hit it.

In my most recent run I collected a wobbly laser and many weapon upgrades for it. I am not exaggerating, I could not see ANYTHING. Some enemies would still survive long enough in there to land a hit and I am virtually defenseless.

To be honest, this feels like Dungreed with slightly better mechanics and much prettier graphics.

But where Dungreed failed, Neon Abyss fails harder. And that is the balance.

If you want to play a rougelite that is almost entirely based on luck, this is the game for you. You never have to feel bad for losing. 

But if you want to progress not just by unlocking and picking new items but in the sense of getting better at the game as the player, this is not at all for you.

Still, I will go ahead and recommend it. Because while I can see that this game isn't right for me, it makes me wish that it was. Whether that means it being more balanced or me having a different taste is of no importance.

for this review i'm going to mostly cover some of the negative reviews since this has a recent "mixed" rating, and i don't feel it deserves it at all.

the review that stood out to me the most, was someone complaining about the difficulty at end-game.
the issue being that after so much progression, a lot of the items become benign or even a hindrance to game-play.

first, you can remove any items from the pool, the user did acknowledge this, but said they didn't want to.
the user is explicitly complaining about the game having too much content, and that content progressively "can" make the game difficult if you don't toggle off any items.

i myself, am very fond of this setup.  i don't need a laser-gun every time i start the dungeon.  in fact the starting gun is rather suitable for game-play, so i don't even really see the issue.

the biggest issue with said review, is that they aren't trying to change game-play for themselves.  they actually can change the game-play for themselves.  they just don't want to and are using their reviews in attempt to remove game-play from everyone else.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1 valid gripe, is lack of viewing item descriptions by default, instead showing you the description "after" you pick the item up.
good news is that there is an item that allows you to see item descriptions, and there is a character that can view descriptions as his ability.

thankfully, there is a really well organized list of items and weapons on a community guide.
but it was a seriously poor decision to lock the mechanic behind a certain character or item.

RNG-
this game does have a good amount of RNG mechanics.  some users list this as a negative, but it's a huge positive for me.  it's just plain fun, and very rarely does something happen that breaks your run.

you can open a treasure chest, it might pop out a coin or few.  it may pop out some grenades or keys.
it might pop out another chest of the same or different type.  and that chest could also carry another chest.
every chest is a dopamine blast because of how varied the contents are.

some doors are a slot machine that you pay a small coin amount to spin.  your chances get better with each attempt, but there's also a chance that the machine blows up leaving you unable to enter that room.
(note these are optional rooms, not the main pathing)

the RNG in this game, to me, is part of the charm.  some runs are harder than others because of it and i love it for that.  again, the RNG very rarely breaks a run, and it's not really broke.  some items are just difficult to use.  like having a mine drop every time you jump.  it's useful, but it limits your mobility as you will get hurt if you land where a mine just dropped.

The game is good right up until the requirements for cursed boss fights.

What has been failed to be understood about action roguelikes is that skill has to mean something. You can't just throw RNG into everything in an attempt to force more runs and extend the longevity of the game. It's lazy design and only serves to undermine skill gained from playing the game long enough.

The game is derivative of other popular roguelikes but does those games worse.

Late into the game, you'll have to fill a wisdom meter in order to enter one of two rooms and hope that the RNG drops a token to proceed to an extra floor by the end. The requirements for them are too much and it gets worse when you have to fill this meter again in said level to fight the next boss.

Add onto this mid minigames, moments of RNG that cost money to get into rooms/chests/spaces, bosses that range from okay to meh and you have a game that falls short of many other roguelikes when it had potential to be as good or better than them.

Progression is the number one thing that needs to be improved for the sequel above all other problems with this game.

That feels like a major waste of an already scarce reward.

But then I reached the end of the game, defeated the boss......... and there's nothing. This game has no real ending, nothing rewarding or providing a feeling of completeness once you've 'won'. All that's left is grinding to unlock other characters and rooms, and I'm not interested.

Why does the Office exist above the bar? I had assumed all along that would be part of the ending or post-completion reward, but it does nothing?

It just feels incomplete.

Roguelike ‎

Neon Abyss from Veewo Games is an innovative roguelike that combines elements from traditional dungeon crawlers with modern aesthetics. Unlike other roguelikes, Neon Abyss offers a colorful pixel art design and a stunning soundtrack crafted by 2-time BAFTA Award winner Danny Baranowsky and an impressive selection of special abilities, weapons, and items that offer an extra layer of depth to the action. Players can explore dungeons filled with enemies, bosses, and loot while ascending each level with progressively more powerful gear and abilities. Fans of the genre will be delighted to find that Neon Abyss also employs challenging roguelike elements such as permadeath and randomly generated levels.

Neon Abyss is an excellent example of a God-tier roguelike. The colorful art style and original soundtrack combine to create an exciting atmosphere that immerses players in the game’s procedurally generated world. With plenty of secrets and new content to discover, it’s a great game for fans of the genre. The roguelike elements work harmoniously together, rewarding skilled players for their strategies and providing an engaging experience for newcomers and veterans alike. Neon Abyss is an excellent roguelike experience that is definitely worth checking out.

GOOD, BAD, UGLY

I'm not recommending this game with the caveat that in the future with some work it could be great. I'll wait for patches before revisiting.

THE GOOD

The game has a high level of polish. The design aspects and vaporwave aesthetics look great. It looks like a finished product. The core mechanics are polished, requiring a good handle on situational awareness along with some enjoyable gunplay.

The soundtrack hits all the right notes. It feels "cool" as you play and really builds on the universe of the game.

Personally, I enjoy the bosses as a whole. While mechanically they aren't complicated and in some cases mimic one another, the sheer chaos is fun. It feels rewarding mastering a boss pattern. Not to mention they look great on screen.

THE BAD

Runs seem to go one of two ways: you either stack up weapon upgrades and/or land a good weapon early or you get stacked with mediocre to bad passive upgrades that have no real meaningful impact on the game. 

The passives are uninteresting. If you don't see movement, damage, range or rate of fire upgrades, most barely move the needle on the gameplay.

Enemy spawns are a problem. They will spawn where you are or will be firing as they spawn and you will take damage. At face value that's bad, but more on that below.

Enemies aren't terribly varied, and the rooms themselves are just a set of platforms. You lack the ability to engage in combat when you struggle on the Y axis due to limits in jump height and character speed, and in many cases you are simply swarmed as a result of beginning in a corner of a room with no chance to move to safety. Alternatively some rooms you never see any danger as you fire comfortably from above or below. Neither is a good look.

Your hitbox is obviously larger than your character. On many occasions you will move or jump in reaction to a projectile in a tight window only to be hit by said projectile. You will see it happen and you will scratch your head.

Large rooms with enemies that blink to your location are frustrating, offering no chance to be mentally prepared beyond simply spamming jump when you enter the room. Enemies off screen engage without your knowledge. This is probably the least frustrating aspect of this game.

THE UGLY

The game relies on a core mechanic of managing one of two types of bars. Purple is "Wisdom" which when full offers a teleport to a room to decide between items. The alternative is "Violence" which operates in a similair vein, only you sacrifice health for a chance at an upgrade. Wisdom is managed by using crystals and avoiding damage. Violence by shooting crystal objects and taking damage when touching them/taking damage in rooms in general.

This would be fine were it not for the way these items you can shoot would not spawn right after a firefight right where you are shooting. Once you shoot a crystal chest, you are now practically locked in on the violence path, which removes your agency. Your pets that follow you will also shoot these crystal items, a system you have next to no control over. Plainly speaking: it's bad design.

The pet system, ooooh the pet system. You will obtain eggs that will hatch (or not) as you clear rooms. Some of these pets are highly beneficial, providing cover from bullets or killing enemies themselves. The real problem comes from negative pets, and as this is a core mechanic to the game, it's just awful for gameplay.

Some pets will snatch up coins before you see them, offering little in return. Some will take hearts, offering a degraded version that can harm you. Some toss grenades constantly, creating a chaotic situation where you are bounced (not damaged) around creating poor positioning you could not control. 

You have no control over this. You either get lucky or don't. That is one of the most infuriating aspects of this title.

Runs either snowball into laughable boomfests or devolve into a long, drawn out but inevitable demise. While that can be the case with some titles in this genre, the best reward players for fighting through the pain and coming out the other side. You CAN win any run, but it feels far less likely than a standard poor Isaac run given all of the other issues around it.

Neon Abyss Review

Basically the level progression of a roguelite, with mostly passive pickups (most weapons have one active ability where you pay something and get something in return). Killing bosses lets you upgrade a tree to get unlocks for future runs (this includes items, tinted rocks, secret rooms, characters).

I love the gunplay, most weapons feel amazing, even the not so good ones, and I like that it doesn't have any ammo system.

Jumping feels a little stiff, but I'm sure that just takes getting used to.

Enemies have good patterns and feel challenging enough, bosses look and feel amazing to beat. If anything it just feels like there isn't that much diversity (I think there are different enemies in later floors, but still).

After 1h of time played (3 runs I think), the best recommendation I can give is buy it if you're into roguelites, isaac, gungeon, etc, or wait for a good sale if you're not into these games. I don't see it dethroning either Isaac or Gungeon, but it's been fun nonetheless and I actually want to try out the other characters and complete my upgrade tree.

This is one of my favorite games because its art style and gameplay are unique. I highly recommend giving this game a try. 9/10

[h1] Game design and Neon Abyss [/h1]

I actually liked this game quite a bit. The problem is, there were... strange, to say the least, design choices. Story is non-existant and that's ok, but gameplay itself feels unpolished and lacking general direction. Here's a list.

1. Items. You can't see what each item does unless you play a specific character, so you have to memorise what each item does - and with how game-changing some of them may be, this is a problem. Items don't stack here; each comes in a single variant. However, a lot of items are either straight up doubles, or give you something on pick up (example: increase weapon damage and get a shield). Each item you get modifies how your character looks, and while fine, you still can't remove that until very late game. 

2. Melee. It is pitiful. Not only you can only control melee attacks as two characters - one performing a standard melee attack and the other using 15's Katana Zero dash (best character) - but if you are not playing the latter it is the worst thing since the invention of knife. Melee works like this: if you're close enough to enemy or box, attacking while aiming close enough will allow character to perform a melee attack, and jesus it is bad. It's a stab without any energy to it, with no proper hitbox id, on very small distance and attacking only forward around character's head's height. Remember Dead Cells? Or Skul? Or any game with some form of melee in it? Yeah, if a game has melee it has a chance of 90% to be better than in this game. The worst thing however, there are a heck ton of items affecting melee which you should never use unless stabbing down boxes, and they all are in the loot tables, and they just exist as clutter - unless you're playing 15 Katana Zero (best character). 

3. Wisdom and Violence. Not only these mechanics are poorly conveyed to the player, they also don't work. The game clearly wants you to get hit as little as possible, but enemies and visual clutter make it difficult. Then, Wisdom rewards no-hits and spending crystals to unlock chests/doors; when you max it out, you can teleport to a special room and pick one of two items. It is pretty neat, however, there is a big but: Violence. You gain Violence by hitting crystal devices and then paying by getting hit; you also increase Violence by getting hit in a room. When you max it out, you can teleport to a special room with 3 (or 4 or 5 - you can upgrade it) items, from which you have to pick one. Once you get it, you lose one max hp, or shield if you don't have hp. Now, the problems with this system are numerous. First of all, to purposely get Violence, you have to allow enemies hit you - and then dodge everything perfectly, because it is triggered only once per room. This especially contrasts with Neon Abyss having challenge rooms, where you need to avoid getting hit to get a reward. It is faster to max out Violence, but it is way more risky due to you spending hp or shields, which in this game are precious resource - and then, after getting hit quite a bit, you have to sacrifice max hp to get a reward. In this sense, Violence requires you to play even more flawlessly than intended flawless route - Wisdom, which is said in-game tips to be harder of the two. Getting hit on purpose can also get extremely annoying. Now, once you progress more in the game, new problem arises: [spoiler] on Ares stage, you have to get full Violence meter to fight Cursed Ares to access final boss, meaning you have to get hit a lot on this stage, and the two resulting boss fights are insanely hard when on low hp/shields. You'd also have to fill up Violence before that - you might choose not to sacrifice max hp, thus gaining no reward at all, but you still spend a lot of hp/shields resource - and after stage 4 you get hit for full heart instead of half [/spoiler]. Also, those routes are mutually exclusive - if you activate a crystal device on Violence it gets transferred to Wisdom, and if you hit crystal device Wisdom converts into violence. Now, crystal chests and special device can spawn in any room, and with gun possible reaching insane power, you end up hitting crystal devices a lot, thus resetting your Wisdom progress. The solution is simply not fire at enemies until you scout the entire room, but avoiding enemies' attacks can become quite a fit. 

4. Cheats. You have to memorise them. They are also not properly explained. And they turn off achievements. 

5. Mini-games. God forbid, mini-games. Claw machine is fine, and even still it throws out of the loop and requires you to play a different game for a bit to get a reward. Do I need to explain that I am playing Neon Abyss, and not FNF?

6. All characters except for egg guy and 15 Katana Zero feel uninspired. They are mostly the same, with some being able to roll, or attack in melee, read items info, or swap weapons - which honestly should be a base for any character. 

7. Moldy hearts. Yes, an entire paragraph just for them: that's how bad they are. If you don't know, moldy hearts are hearts that can either heal you for a heart, or damage you for half a heart or heart after stage 4. The problem is, your character picks them up automatically if your hp isn't full (or even if full? don't remember), leading to a very fun experience. There's a pet which turns normal hearts into moldy hearts - and  you can blacklist it, yes, but why does this exist at all?

8. Weapons have doubles too - including both attack pattern and ability, tho never the exact same, it's all mixed up. Having ability be tied to a weapon may be a good choice, but a lot of weapons simply don't have an ability. 

And that's pretty much it. What? Positives? Okay, tho I won't go too in-depth into them. 
1. Visually, the game is impressive. 
2. First 4 stages feature random bosses buffed up to the stage's level - which is fairly unique and keeps runs from being too same-y.
3. Soundtrack is neat.
4. Bugs are minimal and performance is ok until you become too powerful. 
5. Makes for a nice relaxing experience - until you start feeling pressured into getting all Challenge rooms and maximizing Wisdom. 
6. 15 Katana Zero is here and I couldn't be happier. 

In conclusion, you can get this game. You can buy it. It is quite costy tho. Wouldn't recommend doing so, however. I had quite a bit of fun with it, so maybe you can get it. Maybe not. Makes for a good game design study

I cannot recommend this game, it has too many issues at the present which I’ll outline below.

[b][u]Repetitive[/u][/b] – The whole game is repetitive and a grind. To advance the game, you have to defeat ‘managers’ which are the final level bosses. The first manager is found at the end of level five. After you beat it, an additional level with another manager is unlocked. But you don’t get to advance to the next level straight away, you are forced back to the beginning, and now you have to beat six levels to unlock the next manager. Rinse and repeat until there are eight levels.

After that, you still have to run through all the same levels, but now you have to get to a special room to find a token that drops randomly so that you can access the next two managers. This wouldn’t be so bad if these were optional bosses, but it is necessary to beat them to advance the game.

I’m sorry, but who thought that this was good game design? You play well enough to get to the room, but no token? Guess what? You might as well start a new run grinding through the same levels that you have already played multiple times at this point. Like I said, repetitive. 

[b][u]Music[/u][/b] – For the first couple of runs, the music is ok. But OMG, after several runs it becomes repetitive and grating. For the love of God, please add some more variety to the music! After several runs, I got burnt out on the soundtrack. 

Anyone who says the music is great should reevaluate after 10-15 hours of play. I can almost guarantee that they will change their opinion of the music. Come back after 15 hours and see if you still think the music  is good.

[b][u]Difficult to see some items that can damage you[/u][/b] – Often times there is so much on the screen it is difficult to make out what is damaging you. Not only do you have your own bullets flying around the screen, (often flying in multiple directions at once), you can also have multiple pets that follow you around attacking enemies and firing their own projectiles. (I’m not sure how many pets you can get, but I have had several runs where I have had 20 or more.) 

At the same time you have multiple enemies and their projectiles, not to mention the background which often has flashing elements. In between you, your pets, the enemies, all of the projectiles and flashing background elements, it can become very difficult to see what the hell is damaging you. 


The overall game feels like they made the game and weren’t really sure what direction to take it, so they just started to add stuff to it. They even have an in-game joke about this.

There are other frustrating elements to this game which I won’t go into. But I will say that most of this game's faults become very apparent around the 10-15 hour mark. I think that most of the positive reviews that have less than 15 hours playtime should reevaluate and see if they feel the same way once they hit 15 hours of playtime. 

Due to the game being repetitive and a grind, among other issues, I cannot recommend it.

The guns all have infinite ammo, so that's one less aspect of resource management for those seeking them out.  The massive downside is that you can only ever hold one gun at a time. This makes combos non-existent and the game very unengaging. In fact, there is a character who can specifically combine two weapons into one as a bandaid solution for this very problem, but the way the combination works is just so lazy and unimaginative it's not worth mentioning - just a combination of those two gun sprites shooting both types of bullets at once.

In terms of quality of life, the game actually does most its job well, with remappable everything and difficulty selection anytime in the hub area with no penalty, you can also customize the weapons and passives to disable the garbage you accidentally unlock, so no more Dead Cell BS here.  The one biggest gripe I have, however, is the translation quality. Without mincing words, it's honestly atrocious, combining broken syntax with wrong grammar. While this is mostly limited to the character selection and not item description from what I've seen, it's still grating to see them in-game.

Edit: I have maxed out my gears and unlock all characters by modifying my saves, just to see if the game does increase in variety in the late game as some have said. That is unfortunately not the case for what I described above. Of course, apparently I'm just a guy complaining about the translation quality of another language IN ENGLISH, and not the language that I intend my criticism to reflect, take it with a grain of salt.

Neon Abyss is a roguelike shooter that combines a modern cyberpunk aesthetic with an environmental setting inspired by Greek mythology. 

You start of at the Cerberus bar where you can unlock new gameplay mechanics and characters, browse through your unlocked items and pets, select your character and do some other nifty things (like dancing).

Runs are started by jumping down into the abyss, where you will face randomized rooms filled with various enemies, treasures, shops and puzzles throughout multiple levels in a classic rougelike manner. Every level also features a boss fight, which needs to be defeated to access the next level. As you continue playing you unlock new levels and bosses, as well as cursed forms of previous bosses that require following certain paths to be accessed. 

When it comes to gameplay mechanics, Neon Abyss doesn't reinvent the wheel, but that isn't a requirement for an enjoyable roguelike in my opinion. You collect keys which are used to open locks and bombs which are used to blow stuff up.
Health comes in the forms of heart containers as well as shields, with shields being used up first. An interesting mechanic are pets, which players can hatch from eggs found across the levels. These eggs hatch after clearing a few rooms but might fail to hatch as well. Pets come in various forms, from protective pets to offensive pets and also in the form of pets that collect certain pickups and drop other stuff in exchange. These pets can also level up and become stronger throughout the run, however they also come with their own health and therefore can die.
Killing bosses drops a badge that cycles through various upgrades and boosts your stats in certain ways depending on the badge you end up grabbing.

There are hundreds of different items to be founds and a fair amount of guns as well, however many of the guns exist in multiple forms which end up being the exact same gun but with different active effects. I found quite a few of the guns to be very annoying to use because of strange bullets patterns and because every gun exists in multiple forms you ultimately end up with not thaaat many different guns for a shooter roguelike. 

When killing bosses you unlock faith gems which are used to unlock new gameplay mechanics, rooms, secrets and characters in the aforementioned bar. Each character comes with 2 different "costumes" (if you own the respective DLC) that also grant them different abilities and i found the character variety to be pretty neat, some of them come with very unique playstyles.

However, the part where Neon Abyss falls pretty short is the end game in my opinion. Some of the late game content seems a little rushed and most of the cursed bosses are just different forms of former bosses that feel like bullet sponges in most runs. To get to these cursed bosses you also need to rely on RNG to some degree since you need to follow specific requirements in every run that can easily be messed up. There also are no achievements for killing any of the end game bosses which once again reinforces the feeling of rushed end game content. Also, the screen tends to become very cluttered towards the end of runs as you find many items and pets which can make dodging very hard since you need to stop shooting to even see whats going on.

Neon Abyss also has its fair share of clunky mechanics and bugs (you can't rebind all keys, weapon upgrades cycle in an annoying and unpredictable pattern, elemental effects overwrite each other, the minimap doesn't show all objects, occasional crashes when entering a new level, errors in the English translations and so on). From what I can tell the game is no longer developed and while I wouldn't call it "abandoned" it still could use quite a bit of polishing in its current state.

At the end of the day this is one of those games that make me wish steam had a "mixed feelings" option besides recommending or not recommending a game. Overall I still enjoyed most of my time in the abyss and if you are a roguelike fan then you will probably find some joy in it as well. I would definitely recommend playing all the other top tier roguelikes first (such as Isaac, Spelunky & Gungeon) and if your rougelike itch still isn't satisfied then you can't go wrong with picking up Neon Abyss, although I would recommend doing so during a sale.

While I have enjoyed some of this game and would prefer to give it a neutral review, I'm skewed towards the negative.
This game is very much like Binding of Isaac, sharing many of the positives and all of the negatives.
It also tries to put its own spin on a lot of it, ultimately coming out all the worse for it.
Take the 2D perspective for example, while it has been shown to work by plenty of other roguelikes, Neon Abyss' characters limited mobility, bad level design and unfair enemy placement/types make it significantly less fun. It takes many elements of all of these things directly from BoI without really considering how well it works in 2D, resulting in an overall frustrating experience.
Run variety, one of the most important factors of a roguelike and something that BoI in particular excels at, is also abysmal in Neon Abyss. The reasons for this are the lack of item variety and Neon Abyss trying to reinvent the wheel with new systems.
Guns in particular significantly limit variety, where in BoI you just had basic tear projectiles to start with, you had a wide variety of items that completely transformed how they work and look, in Neon Abyss that is mostly achieved with guns.
There are many different guns that all work somewhat differently, however they have very little synergy with items.
You can get items that increase damage, projectiles, range, firing speed or add a chance to shoot additional projectiles with different properties, however your gun will still fire the same mechanically.
For some this is a positive as you can always just switch your gun out for a different one mid-run, but ultimately this significantly limits item variety as none of them can fundamentally change how you fire each gun.
Another thing Neon Abyss takes and ruins from BoI is the familiar system. In Binding of Isaac there was a category of items that granted you a (most of the time) invulnurable familiar that followed you and helped you in various ways, like shooting enemies or dropping items for you.
Neon Abyss instead has the egg system, where you can pick up egg pickups that over the course of a couple of cleared rooms have a chance to become a familiar. these familiars work in much the same as BoI aside from one key difference: they can be killed. Whether it be by enemies, projectiles or traps, if your familiar takes enough damage it will die and that's that. This feels like a complete downgrade from the familar system in the most frustrating ways. Eggs more often than not fail to hatch, and even when they do, chances are the familiar you get isn't any good anyways, and even on the off chance that they are, if you aren't particularly careful and having a great run, they'll get killed anyways.
Finally a third feature that I feel is a straight up worse version of something in BoI is the faith system.
Where in BoI you had Devil Rooms and Angel Rooms, special post-boss rooms that rewarded you for not taking any damage per floor with great items, Neon Abyss exchanges that for a faith system.
Now you have to rely on crystal items (chests, doors, etc.) to get the process going, where you activate said item with crystals that you pick up to fill up the "angel" side of the bar, or damage it and let it deal damage to you to fill up the "devil" side of the bar.
You can then also fill up said bar by either not taking any damage for each cleared room for the angel side, or taking damage each room for the devil side. This would not be an issue at all save for one important detail, only one side of the bar can exist at a time.
As you might strive for angel rooms as those align with not wanting to take damage anyway, you might happen to accidentally damage a crystal item, either by shooting it mid-fight with enemies or having your familiars shoot it with no input from you. This results in your faith bar instead getting changed to the devil side with a lot less of the bar filled up, essentially wasting all your effort and forcing you to either abandon that mechanic until you find another crystal and start over or force yourself to keep taking damage for devil rooms.
This is one of the most frustrating aspects of the game.
As you keep trying to do no damage runs for extra items, which is already frustrating enough with the level design and enemies in this game, now you also have to contend with crystals being obstacles in every other stage where your already flawed and fragile familiars are now an active threat to your run.
This is a major issue in a game like this that heavily relies on items to make it fun and exciting, when the vast majority of the ones you get being nearly useless or incredibly situational, every chance at an additional item is crucial for having a good time and saving a run.
This could have very well been a great game but the devs insisted on trying to change mechanics that already worked incredibly well in their main inspiration for significantly worse versions of themselves, making this game a lot more frustrating than it is fun.
If you don't mind bashing your head against the wall for that one god run where you destroy everything then this might be for you, otherwise save yourself the trouble and find another roguelike.

The games first impression is so much fun! It is your typical rougelike game, lots of weapons, lots of upgrades, lots of enemies and randomly generated dungeons.

There are so many good upgrades, if you get a good run, you'll feel invincible, while other runs can feel impossible. There are a lot of negative combinations for items aswell, so as long as you don't know what which item does, you'll suddenly end up for example with explosive shots that constantly kill yourself, because you got no item yet to protect you from your own explosions, but your weapon hits the entire screen.

It does get repetitive after a while, as you'll always play through the same levels and same bosses until you encounter the last, a new boss for each run. There isn't much new stuff in terms of the story, just jump in, do the next run! The runs take about an hour, can be much longer if you get loads of money and play all the minigames with it. Would have prefered it to be a bit shorter like it was the first few runs tbh. So why is it getting longer after the first runs? Because at first it stops at level 5, then level 6, then 7 and lastly you get until level 8/9 for the last bosses. These last bosses also have special conditions for meeting them, so you might not even get it done to get to them in the run.

The one thing, I feel like makes this game harder than it should, is how many weapons and upgrades boost not only your damage, but your visuals aswell. Your shots get bigger, they multiply, they bounce around. Sometimes makes it impossible to see enemy projectiles. Occasionally I get such big shots, can't even see the big bosses in their rooms, because my weapons just blank out the entirety of the screen. I just keep firing and hope that they die, before I die, because I can't see what they're even doing.

Because of these things, the first few times playing this, feel more fun imo. Even though you have no idea whats going on, you can at least still follow it and are done with a run quicker aswell. I have not yet played the the sequel to this game, I wanted to start with this one, but it definitely sold me on getting it!

Even though you can select different difficulty options, it also has another type of difficulty changes going on. If you win lots of times in a row, you get harder runs, if you lose, you get easier ones. There are little dots over the difficulty setting showing you how hard your setting is. It ranges from 1 to 5 dots. 5 dots on easy are even harder than 1 dot on normal. I don't know where exactly it changes, but it is something to keep in mind. Or maybe you can just lose a few runs on purpose, if you don't like how hard its gotten. I liked the difficulty on normal, but I have not been able to clear all the bosses. I am giving up here, as I don't like doing 1 hour runs, just to not be able to get to the right boss at the end, or if I do get the right boss, not have enough hearts to survive the fight.. I guess, I am simply not good enough, but I had my fair share of fun!

Truly want to like this game, but I just can't. There are so many rogue-likes that do better what this game is trying to achieve.
The enemy diversity is abysmal.
Melee damage upgrades are a joke, if you don't get items that let you reach flying enemies
Way too based on pop culture references instead of originality
Manager system is okay with choosing target end boss for your run, except getting to the last managers requires heavy rng and the fact that you have to beat every previous manager during the run (Screw Hal and his 2 phase bullet hell BS and him being much harder than the next supposedly harder boss)
Faith system is a neat idea, one being reached by activating crystals normally and not taking damage and the other for taking damage and sacrificing health.
Except that getting an item from the red bonus room requires you to lose even more health by permanently losing a heart container. And you need to do this to have a small chance on getting a medal which allows you to fight the 4th manager. (Why is a progression boss locked behind so much damaging rng!?)
And the unlock system is such a grind. You need memory crystals and to unlock a new character you need like 15. But you only get 1 per beaten boss. And it is an unlock tree so you have to use up your crystals for other stuff first and you need about 30 crystals on the fastest way to the character unlock. This unfun grind makes me wanna scream.

Well, I'm conflicted. This game is honestly incredibly fun, and fairly unique. Plenty of references and tongue in cheek call-outs to other games/series/movies etc. 
Pros:
-Colorful lighting is very aesthetically pleasing
-Fantastic Music score, slaps
-Interesting enemy types/patterns. You have to pay attention to which enemies spawn where
-Interesting bosses, learning their patterns was fun, specifically the managers.
-Fun items and Guns (Like i said, references and the character model changes are fun!)

Cons:
-Some rooms feel like damage is unavoidable, and a few enemies spawn inside you sometimes (especially in challenge rooms.
-Game is honestly incredibly easy. I failed 2 total runs between playing the tutorial and finishing the game, and that was because explosive bullets caused me to suicide.
-Enemies, while varied, don't seem to have a pattern. You'll fight the same enemies in the first room your explore that you fight one room before  [spoiler] Ares/Athena fight. [/spoiler] 
-The wisdom crystal/chest can be triggered by enemies. Often, it'll spawn and instantly get hit by an enemy bullet, ruining your buildup to the particular room.

Overall, I give this game a 7.5/10, with a few suggestions that are entirely personal.
1) Make the wisdom crystals/chests NOT triggerable by enemies, the RNG on that isn't fair or fun.
2) The ability to make your character model smaller via items (or even a crouch feature?) would allow for better dodging ability.
3)Possibly changing the enemy types as you get further, (or [spoiler] in the specific Ares/Athena floors [/spoiler] ) as the game feels like one long level till the end.

half a good game, half RNG trash. 
The movement is janky but once you figure out how to alter your controls to what works, it gets better. I found it hard to play on keyboard. There are no mouse options to speed up the mouse, and I don't want to alter my mouse settings in windows every time I play. That should be standard if you expect people to use a mouse. I found controller to be much more natural feeling. However, using LT as the jump button took some getting used to. If you do the controller method just know, you can remove up on the D-pad as jump and just use LT. This seemed to work much better for me, at least. But, with controller shooting is atrocious. There isn't much lock on so you will have to manually aim most shots and the enemies move very quickly so it can get annoying quick.  
To the guns. The starter guns are awful. You literally need any other weapon other than the starting weapon. Most are good, however, there isn't much option to try out new ones on runs. You just don't find them in the wild enough. Most times when you find a gun it is an option between a gun and a powerup, and it just makes more sense to use that for the powerup and hope you get a gun only room (rare) or have extra coins to just buy one for the shop.  
The starting characters are not too bad, outside the rythym melee girl riding the plushy (IDK, it looks dumb and plays dumber).  The other characters are fine (robot can be annoying without being able to use hearts). 
Melee is broken. It does not work. I have tried to melee enemies and I literally cannot. The character will either hit over the enemy or not attempt the hit at all. Then if you are the melee starting character riding the plushy, then you just automiss most things because you are too tall. Same goes with the powerups that make your character bigger on screen. This leads into one of the boss fights where they expect you to stand under and over laser beams but your character is too big and just gets hit automatically. 
There are too many RNG based things that are just useless. There are chests where you can take damage to open them, and damage, as you can imagine is something you are trying to avoid. However, when the chest opens all you get is some crystals (which over drop and are useless most of the time).  The jackpot doors can go screw themselves. There are doors that you have to pay to spin a roulette wheel to open. If you get 3 in a row you open the door, but then you have to pay in the next thing as well to start the activity....so it just gets frustrating when you are spending 30 coins just to open the door to play the minigame once just to get the crappy minigame and lose the rest of your coins. 
The minigames, the only one that seems reasonable and worth it is the piano jumping. It is easy, you can do it most times, given you have anyone but the plushy rider, but the others are terrible. Fishing is easy but rewards you nothing, and the claw game is just stupid because there is no skill that can be applied just hit hope and pray (in the trailer it makes it seem like the claw goes up and down quickly, it does not, and half the time the bomb and the claw sync up in speed so you just end up having to wait and wait and wait). 
Pets get annoying because it just helps to get you lost in the map. Not all the pets stay behind you, some wander and most times i'm wondering if it is an enemy or a friend, and if the projectile is from a friend or foe. Just ends up being clutter that makes it more difficult to discern what is happening.  
So, to what I did like, some of the boss fights were good, although some attacks really come at your quick without much warning, so if you are jumping while the attack starts you will likely just get hit.
The best part of the game is the guns, it was good to shoot them when you didn't have to worry about a tiny bullet hitting a moving target with a controller and no aiming help.  The variety of weapons was good and they all seemed pretty different in function. 
But ya, once you get the jumping with LT and the shooting with R3 it becomes playable, but just gets bogged down in all the annoying extra crap. 
Also, starting at the bottom right or left side of the screen is an issue because you end up getting pinned there very easily. Becomes the enemies just appear and you don't have any indication what they will be so you have to analyze the entire battlefield instantly to decipher what is going to shoot a lob shot, vs a laser shot, vs a melee charge, vs a midair split shot, vs a laser that just follows you around the screen. 
I am thumbing this down because I would not recommend this game to anyone who doesn't already like this genre so much they are willing to play anything (like me).
I have more comments but I think you get the gist.

Progress losing bugs! This is an incredibly fun game but there are bugs that destroy progression.

Old bugs that have been in the game for years have not been fixed, and now the devs have moved on to another project (the sequel game). Even worse, some of those bugs are game-breaking. I currently cannot progress because the bugs prevent me from doing so because they force me to restart my runs all of the time. The bug I get stuck with most often is one that makes me unable to jump down/move down through platforms - this often causes me to get stuck with no way to move through rooms because seemingly impassable platforms (which should be traversible) block the way, forcing a restart. And it keeps happening, almost every run. That is not fun, and that is not what I paid for.

To clarify: Changing my controls settings doesn't help, and no buttons on my keyboard help whenever this bug happens - I've tried pressing all of them. The game even shows that my controls are supposedly set up correctly, but when this bug happens no button or button combination on my keyboard allows me to go down through platforms like I should be able to. And due to the game giving me random rooms on my route, I have no control over whether the route of a run will have rooms that have sections where I will need to fall down through a platform to progress, and such rooms are very common.

Hopefully soon the devs will wake up and give this game some much-needed maintenance, but until then I cannot play the game and I cannot give this game a positive review. And this whole situation really doesn't make me very optimistic about the sequel.

Also, when you open the game for the first time it will open up a webpage that goes to the sequel's Store Page. That is not cool, especially when the first game doesn't work.

Neon Abyss is a great addition to the roguelike genre, honestly being one of my favorites to date. I may be a little biased because I love anything neon/cyberpunkish, but damn, this game is so aesthetically pleasing.

The combat and gunplay is very interesting with each perk you get influencing the way your weapon shoots and the damage it does. There are plenty of weapons to try out and explore, each with a special ability that makes trying new weapons intriguing to the player. I cannot tell you how many times I picked up a new weapon and my relics modified it to a point that I just had a huge smile on my face and was laughing out loud and what the bullets did and how hectic it looked like.

The rooms throughout the dungeons were not really anything to keep in mind. It was usually the same rooms randomly generated with the same atmosphere and chests. The only rooms that looked different were boss rooms, which I can attest, looked amazing.

The enemies were also not much varied. Same enemies in the same rooms made it easy to predict what enemies would be in a room depending on the room layout. I noticed a review stating that they were getting hit off screen and couldn't see enemies, but I learned what enemies would spawn in a room and just to always be focused on the bullet spray hell that was happening(ya know, as in ALL roguelikes).

Overall, it is a simple roguelike with only 6 manager bosses, which I managed to defeat on Normal in about 10 hours, but it could definitely be done in less, given the luck on weapons, keys, etc. I would definitely check Neon Abyss out if you are a fan of roguelikes like I am.

There is a reason that even hyper-experienced Isaac players play with the item description mod, and the creators wisely allow this without impacting achievements.  Not even mega-fans want to memorize what 400 different items do, when the majority of them have no indication of what they actually do based off the name and picture.

This is 2022.  Anyone can alt-tab out of the game and look up what the items do.  The crime is that you SHOULD do this, and the developers are pompous assholes for forcing this awful, game-disrupting practice to be a regular feature of the game.  Putting an item in the game to identify other items is not a solution, it is a waste of an item slot.

They ripped off just about everything else from other games, mostly Isaac, but basic quality of life improvements got chucked.  The item descriptions are IN THE GAME CODE, they can be looked up online, but they hide them from you anyway, because reasons?  It's an annoying waste of time that is shoehorned into every single run, and it kills the game.

A lot of the items are just absolute garbage, and you shouldn't bother trying to predict what items do based off the name/pic; 90% of the time there is no relation whatsoever.  There are like 50 items that manipulate worthless angry sprites, and only 2 or 3 of them are any good.  You will get flooded with crap that buffs these sprites when you have no way to generate them, or tons of ways to generate them but they have a cap and are pretty much useless without buffs anyway.

The addition of the ability to ban items seems like such an elegant solution... except that there are 400 freaking items, and  you can only ban FIVE before it disables achievements.  That's not enough to take even one shitty mechanic out of the pool; all you can do is take out a couple pieces of one garbage-tier set, which only serves to make the other 20 items with that mechanic even worse, since they lose pieces of their synergy chain.  That five seriously needs a zero in front of it to make it worthwhile.

The bafflingly stupid decision to keep item descriptions hidden is like the developers playing chicken with their own player-base, and then ripping off their steering wheel.  Like, they KNOW that we can and will look them up by alt-tabbing... Are they REALLY going to make us go through that hassle?  Wouldn't it be better for everyone to NOT make us do this, since it hurts our experience and thus THEIR game reviews?  Are they really going to die on this hill of non-information, forcing their game quality to suffer for the sake of not getting with the times and accepting that any and all game information can and will acquired by players that want it?  Players ARE going to find this info (that IS ALREADY PROGRAMMED IN THE GAME), wouldn't it be better for everyone to just make it a feature?

To all of these questions, the developers have one answer: Fuck you.  Not one single player picks up this game and says: "wow, I think it's really neat that the developers hide the item descriptions from me, this randomness is so fun!".  A workaround exists, it is usable by everyone, but is a pain in the ass, and they force that on you anyway, because the developers have their heads so far up their asses that they would rather people suffer than play the game the way THEY don't want you to play it.

Some other quick points:

- The crystals are worthless, why do they even exist?  You might be able to use maybe 5 to 10 on a given level (if you are actively trying), and they give you 20+.  They have a ton of items to 'help' generate more crystals, when basically every map ends with a full crystal bar and a dozen crystals lying on the ground because you can only carry 5.  Some guns let you use the crystals effectively, but those guns are usually either so overpowered that you don't need to worry about it, or so underpowered that you may as well ignore the feature.

- No damage numbers, only bosses have health bars.  Makes it even harder to differentiate between guns and figure out what's actually good.  Another egregious example of intentionally hiding key information for its own sake.

- Grenades are really just another type of key.  Despite their attempts to make items to support using them in combat, you won't and shouldn't.  

- The egg and follower system is pure rng, not explained at all, completely unable to be customized or controlled, and the line of eggs makes it almost impossible to see any projectiles on the screen in the mid to late game.

- The unlockable minigames are not balanced at all.  Do yourself a favor and only unlock the claw game, because it is stupidly easy and lets you actually choose what you want once you get good.  The rest are way harder and completely random.  The dance room is a joke, it is so much harder than the others.  


This game is derivative trash, and the fact that it makes fun of itself for this doesn't change that fact.  The things it rips off ate all better than it.  The developers actively ignore the unending complaints of their player base, and think that forced time-wasting in every item room is a feature.  Do not support these assholes, let them take their ball and go home and play with themselves, since that is their design philosophy.

It's a shame I have to leave a negative review, because Neon Abyss is a game I really wanted to like. Right out of the gate, though, it feels slow, quiet, and uninspired. I found a lot of QoL issues in the demo, but figured that build's about 8 months old, so that's not really too much of an issue- but save for one, they're all still present in the base game.

Within 40 minutes of playing, I found the following problems:
[list]
[*]Here's one of the big ones- you can't teleport from any room to a room with the teleporter. What's the point? Teleporters are intended to reduce backtracking, right? They're still "reducing backtracking" but you still have to backtrack to the actual teleporter. The way Gungeon does it, where you can go to any teleporter at will, or Monolith, where you can go to any [i]room[/i] at will, is perfect. I see no reason to deviate from that idea.
[*]Eggs are... weird. It's not like in Isaac where they closely follow your movements, they instead flip direction entirely once you look the other way.
[*]Music restarts every. Single. Room. If you enjoy listening to the same 30 seconds of the "intense" version of the track, then more power to you, but a Gungeon-esque system would've been better, where the track only reverts back to ambient after a minute or so.
[*]Item text persists only for a couple seconds, and you usually don't have enough time to read what the gun or familiar does.  This isn't like Isaac where descriptions are two or three words, this is two or three sentences. It's inconvenient to have to go to the pause menu every time I see something with longer text.
[*]I think I got an event of some kind at one point, but I couldn't read what it said because, sure enough, the item text showed up as a familiar evolved, and I completely missed what the event said since the item splash text is so large that it covered up a good third of the screen.
[/list]

The trailers will have you believe this is a fast paced, Gungeon-esque game, and I was hoping this would scratch the Gungeon itch, but instead it just makes that itch worse. Instead of taking the positives of Gungeon (its humor, polish, core gameplay loop, balance) it seems to take the negatives (visually busy design, pacing, pre-update slow backtracking) while offering almost nothing new to the table. Babies are a neat concept, but even they aren't completely polished, and that's the game's only standout factor- I had a baby that split into about 10 zombie babies, and it was never explained why- I had to go to the pause menu to figure it out. I never saw the actual health of the zombie babies either, and the item text implies it would just continually split itself, which I figured wasn't right, and sure enough they all died a few seconds later.

I feel like Neon Abyss doesn't know what it wants to be. It wants to be Isaac, it wants to be Enter the Gungeon, but what it lacks from those two games is staying power. I put this in the same category as Steredenn and Wizard of Legend, where they're games I really wanted to like, but out of the gate i saw pacing and polish issues that I just can't overlook. I'm willing to overlook problems with a game if it's fun, because no game is perfect, but Neon Abyss... isn't fun.

A game being derivative is okay and expected in today's industry. Monolith, for example, is one of my favorite roguelites, and it's just about one of the most derivative roguelites you're going to find. This is derivative for the wrong reasons. Where Monolith takes existing ideas, iterates on them, and seamlessly integrates them together into a cohesive experience, Neon Abyss feels like it's taking existing ideas, throwing them in, and praying it works, and the way I see it, it doesn't work.

I think this game has the potential to be good, but it's going to take a lot of changes. The game, overall, needs faster pacing (at the very least optional like in Gungeon) and needs to be able to stand by itself, as well as a lot of quality of life iteration. If i found this many gripes in 40 minutes, that tells me there's probably a lot of others, too.
